title: Generating Change: A Global Survey of What News Organisations Are Doing with AI
pub: JournalismAI, POLIS, London School of Economics and Political Science
author: Charlie Beckett · Mira Yaseen

However, it does not address legal use, authoritative grounding, lawyer or judicial verification, supervision, or responsibility, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: Although focused on journalism rather than legal services, the source supports the cluster’s implementation-centred proposition: useful AI capability does not itself ensure reliable or accessible delivery. It identifies language, cultural fit, funding, expertise and human review as practical constraints, while treating reduced disparities as a cautious hope rather than a demonstrated outcome.
qs: Most tools are made for English speakers, which causes accessibility challenges to both non- English speakers and English speakers with non-Western accents.

Respondents gave us several examples where they discovered issues using AI tools in non- English languages or non-Western English accents:           Coral has been very successful as a comment moderation tool, but we still find the      ‘grey’ area comments require a human element, especially as it is an American tool not      built for the South African audience in mind.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The newsroom evidence aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: AI delivers uneven benefits across tasks, requires continuing human intervention, and creates value through selective workflow and role redesign rather than wholesale worker replacement. Its non-representative, cross-industry evidence is corroborative rather than direct evidence about legal practice.
qs: 1.5 What is Working and What is Not Overall, the successful use of AI technologies varied widely among respondents, though transcription and audio-editing tools were seen as advantageous by many.

kp.k: Survey maps uneven global newsroom AI adoption
kp.d: The report draws on a survey of 105 news and media organisations in 46 countries, supplemented by interviews and conference conversations conducted between April and July 2023. It explicitly states that the sample is not globally representative and primarily captures the perceptions of people leading AI development or application inside participating organisations.
qs: It is based on a survey of 105 news and media organisations from 46 different countries regarding AI and associated technologies.
The surveys and interviews were conducted between April and July, 2023.

We do not claim that the survey is representative of the global industry – that would be almost impossible on an international scale – nor does it equally reflect all viewpoints within the different parts of news organisations.

kp.k: AI already spans the journalism value chain
kp.d: More than 75% of respondents reported using AI somewhere across newsgathering, production, or distribution. Reported applications include transcription, text extraction, trend detection, fact-checking, proofreading, summarisation, code generation, recommendation systems, personalisation, social-media scheduling, chatbots, and search optimisation.
qs: More than 75% of respondents use AI in at least one of the areas across the news value chain of news gathering, production and distribution.
These areas – newsgathering, news production and news distribution – cover all the content creation stages from ideation to publishing.
Around 80% of respondents reported using AI technologies in news distribution, a slightly smaller percentage compared to production, but the range of use cases was the widest.

kp.k: Efficiency is the dominant adoption objective
kp.d: More than half of respondents identified efficiency and productivity as principal reasons for adopting AI. The intended mechanism is to automate repetitive or laborious work, accelerate production, and reallocate journalists toward creative, investigative, field-based, or otherwise complex work; one respondent cautioned that newsroom conversations focused on speed rather than quality.
qs: More than half cited increasing efficiency and enhancing productivity as core objectives driving their adoption of AI.
They said they hoped to automate monotonous and repetitive tasks, thereby streamlining workflows and allowing journalists to engage in “more creative, relevant, and innovative work”
Almost all our use cases for AI are to speed up news production. It’s always about speeding up, I don’t think I’ve had one conversation about using it to improve quality.
Freeing up time for journalists to continue doing their job is the greatest impact achieved.

kp.k: AI changes work before eliminating it
kp.d: Respondents with operational experience described AI as redistributing and reshaping work rather than simply removing it. Automation reduces manual scheduling, curation, monitoring, and routine writing, while increasing responsibility for setting rules, supervising systems, interpreting outputs, and managing broader outcomes.
qs: AI streamlines workflows, but it doesn’t replace work entirely. It changes the nature of the work and expands our impact.
AP’s NLG of earnings reports nearly a decade ago liberated our reporters from the grind of churning out rote earnings updates and freed them up to do more meaningful journalism.

Many respondents said AI integration is changing existing roles within the newsroom through training and upskilling. Along the same lines, AI is changing the nature of a journalist’s role and sought after skills.

kp.k: Most organisations report limited present workflow impact
kp.d: Almost 75% of respondents in earlier adoption stages had not yet observed a noticeable workflow impact, although many expected future effects as AI takes over mundane tasks. Similarly, around 60% said AI had not yet affected existing newsroom roles, making the report’s workforce conclusions chiefly evidence about current perceptions and expectations rather than measured displacement.
qs: The vast majority of respondents, almost 75%, who are still in the early stages of AI adoption, have not witnessed a noticeable impact yet, but expect to in the future:
Responses to whether AI technologies impacted existing roles in newsrooms followed a similar pattern; around 60% said AI integration has not done so.
Not yet because it’s a transition still in early stages. AI is augmenting rather than totally changing roles.

kp.k: New roles combine editorial and technical capabilities
kp.d: Some organisations reported creating AI management, data-analysis, and cross-functional positions, while others expected roles such as prompt engineers, machine-learning engineers, data scientists, and news technologists. More commonly, organisations were adapting existing jobs through AI literacy, data skills, prompt design, and closer collaboration between journalists and engineers.
qs: Some newsrooms said AI integration has led to the creation of new roles related to AI in a variety of areas, such as data analytics:
Not yet, but we are working on new vacancies for AI that include Prompt engineers, AI and ML engineers, and data scientists.

Noticeably, many organisations underscored that AI integration is changing existing roles within the organisation, through training and upskilling in AI literacy and specific skills like data analysis or prompt engineering, rather than creating entirely new roles:
Yes, we have created at least one new role focused on managing AI experiences, and expect we may have more, but the growth is slow and deliberate.

kp.k: Hiring demand shifts toward AI-enabled workers
kp.d: Respondents predicted changing hiring criteria and demand for workers able to combine journalism with effective AI use. Views on employment diverged: some expected leaner newsrooms and job losses, while others argued that AI would redefine roles and increase demand for people who can use the tools productively.
qs: I think the impact has been more felt in considering who to hire and who not to hire. I would need less writers once AI is deployed.
It may mean job losses because the work is currently being done by say five people, and may only need one person.
We believe AI isn’t a threat to jobs. But people who learn to effectively use AI to leverage their work will be in demand, and soon many roles will expect people to be able to use these tools.
Others said that AI will not “replace jobs.” Rather, AI will redefine the role of journalists; “steering AI… requires new competencies and new functions.”

kp.k: Institutional AI strategy remains uncommon
kp.d: Around one-third of respondents had or were developing an institutional AI strategy, a proportion similar to the 2019 survey. Approaches ranged from organisation-wide reviews and dual vendor/in-house development to case-by-case deployment; absent strategies were often attributed to competing priorities, scarce resources, or reliance on individual enthusiasts rather than lack of interest.
qs: Around 1/3 of the respondents said their organisation had an AI strategy or were currently developing one, similar to the results we saw in our 2019 survey.
Our organisation does not have a formal strategy for AI-related activities. We rely on the initiative and enthusiasm of some of our colleagues who are interested in AI.
Some respondents said they adopt a case-by-case approach to AI, without necessarily developing a particular institutional level strategy.
We partner with vendors that are moving fast, so we can move quickly, too. Meanwhile, we are building in-house capabilities so we can have control and ownership.

kp.k: Financial and technical barriers constrain adoption
kp.d: Financial constraints and technical difficulties remained the leading adoption barriers, especially for smaller organisations unable to hire specialist staff, fund training, or integrate tools with existing systems. More experienced and better-resourced organisations increasingly focused on compatibility and interoperability, indicating different adoption stages across the sample.
qs: As we saw in our 2019 report, financial constraints and technical difficulties remain the most pressing challenges for integrating AI technologies in the newsroom.
Smaller and emerging news organisations often struggle to allocate the necessary funding to hire qualified personnel to implement and maintain AI systems.

Newsrooms with several years of experience with AI integration in the newsroom mentioned specifically the challenge of achieving compatibility and interoperability with existing systems and platforms:
We are a mid-sized regional nonprofit startup with a strong engineering team and an innovative organisational culture… But, we have nowhere near the technical power of large national organisations.

kp.k: Rapid change demands continuous organisational adaptation
kp.d: Respondents consistently identified the pace of AI development as a strategic problem: tools may become outdated, integrations require substantial setup, and organisations must repeatedly revise plans, training, and evaluation. Hands-on experimentation reportedly produced more realistic expectations about capabilities, limitations, resources, and near-term substitution risks.
qs: The challenge of keeping pace with the rapid evolution of AI was consistently mentioned throughout the survey.
The technologies are evolving so quickly it’s difficult to know what technology to take on for fear it will soon be outdated.
Our approach became more realistic taking into consideration our resources and the very fast involvement in the industry.
For those who have hands-on experience, there is more enthusiasm about the future, and less fear about AI replacing journalists’ work, at least in the near term.

kp.k: Human oversight remains a central operating principle
kp.d: Journalists and media makers continued to favour a human-in-the-loop model, particularly for verification, fact-checking, contextualisation, and editorial judgment. The report presents oversight as necessary because generative systems can fabricate information, reproduce bias, and lack the contextual interpretation expected in journalism.
qs: Journalists and mediamakers continued to stress the need for a ‘human in the loop approach,’ in line with the results in our 2019 survey.
No matter how advanced AI becomes, human criteria will always be essential in the whole fact-checking process.
Context and interpretation is everything in our industry, and this is something that AI technologies will struggle to duplicate.
Test, iterate, repeat. Experiment and scale but always with human oversight and management.

kp.k: Ethical concerns focus on trust and accountability
kp.d: More than 60% of respondents expressed concern about effects on editorial quality and journalism, including accuracy, fairness, independence, transparency, verification, privacy, data ethics, and human judgment. Respondents called for explainable systems, newsroom disclosure where AI explicitly generates content, and adaptable ethical guidelines, while the report notes uncertainty about which routine AI-assisted processes warrant disclosure.
qs: More than 60% of respondents expressed concerns about the ethical implications of AI integration for editorial quality and other aspects of journalism.
The adoption of AI in journalism raises potential concerns related to bias, editorial independence, transparency, verification, data ethics, and human judgement.
They called for transparency from the designers of AI systems as well as transparency from those who apply the systems, such as newsrooms.
So it is not clear where the line is drawn between an AI-assisted production process that requires disclosure and one that does not.

kp.k: Bias mitigation is difficult and resource-intensive
kp.d: Although respondents broadly accepted the need to address algorithmic bias, few supplied concrete debiasing practices. Examples included evaluation frameworks, modifying training data, overriding recommender outputs with rules, red-team analysis, and ethical committees; respondents characterised implementation as technically complex, multidisciplinary, time-consuming, and difficult for small AI teams.
qs: Setting de-biasing techniques emerged as a highly challenging area for most respondents.

Firstly, we check both recommender systems and NLP applications for basic types of bias via an evaluation framework. Secondly, we mitigate unwanted bias e.g. by changing training data for NLP systems or introducing rules that override the raw output of recommender systems.
We have tested an approach where a red-team analyses the algorithms in order to find biases on them.
However this kind of work is resource-consuming and it is very difficult to implement it properly in newsrooms because of the small size of the AI teams involved.

kp.k: Generative AI experimentation is already widespread
kp.d: Around 85% of respondents had experimented with generative AI by mid-2023, using it for code, images, summaries, headlines, search optimisation, data extraction, translation, and brainstorming. Adoption remained heterogeneous: some newsrooms used it daily, while others deliberately excluded direct content generation or employed it to demonstrate bias and inaccuracy in media-literacy training.
qs: The vast majority of respondents, around 85% at least, have experimented with genAI technologies at varying degrees and in a range of ways as you’ll see in the responses below.
We use them on a daily basis for various tasks, such as summarising articles, evaluating content quality, search engine optimisation, and generating copy.
We are using it but not to generate content. We have experimented with ChatGPT for analysing large swaths of data.
Some are apprehensive about using genAI in editorial tasks, while others are using them regularly in coding, headline generation, and search engine optimisation.

kp.k: Generative AI lowers technical adoption barriers
kp.d: Almost three-quarters of respondents believed generative AI offered opportunities beyond traditional AI, especially for copy generation, personalisation, research, and brainstorming. They attributed this to accessible interfaces, reduced need for specialist programming, faster responses, and an ability to work with large amounts of information, although these were respondent assessments rather than comparative performance tests.
qs: There was a high level of agreement among the respondents; almost 3/4 agree with this statement, particularly with respect to assisting journalists in “generating copy,” like summaries and headlines, personalised distribution, and research and brainstorming:
GenAI seems to require a lot less technical skills to the end user with much faster response times, allowing us to bring it to fruition quickly throughout the organisation.
GenAI can change the way we interact with information, allowing us to grasp massive amounts of data, and level the playing field between high and low data skills.

kp.k: Generative AI raises misinformation risks
kp.d: Respondents were divided on whether generative AI creates categorically new challenges: 52% were unsure and 40% said it did. A recurring argument was that generative AI intensifies familiar problems—bias, opacity, privacy, and inaccuracy—by increasing the scale and potential harm of fabricated or manipulated content, thereby increasing the need for human verification and more sophisticated validation methods.
qs: Slightly over half the respondents, 52%, were not sure if this was the case , whereas 40% did view genAI as presenting new challenges in the newsroom.
However, they think genAI technologies exacerbate to a considerable degree those challenges, therefore potentially producing more harm:
GenAI will allow the production and distribution of disinformation at a scale we haven’t seen before – this will potentially impact news consumption. but also send people to more trusted sources.
I am very concerned about the generation of content without verification.

kp.k: AI may intensify commercial and trust pressures
kp.d: Respondents feared AI could enable mass-produced clickbait, polarising material, reduced editorial standards, and further commercialisation at a time of declining public trust. The report also identifies a prospective disintermediation risk: audiences may obtain information directly from chatbots rather than news organisations, forcing journalism to demonstrate its distinctive social value.
qs: There are fears that AI technologies would further commercialise journalism, boosting poor quality and polarising content, leading to a further decline in public trust in journalism.
I think it’s going to result in a lot of mass-produced clickbait as news organisations compete for clicks.
GenAI has also however created the threat of ‘disintermediation’ for the news media. Why should people go to a news organisation for information if they can just prompt a chatbot?
In a world of machine-created information, much of it unreliable, responsible, public service journalism is in a great position to prove its value.

kp.k: Global South newsrooms face compounded barriers
kp.d: The report argues that AI’s benefits are concentrated in the Global North and that Global South newsrooms face more pronounced resource, infrastructure, skills, language, legal, and political constraints. Examples include low internet penetration, difficulty hiring technical experts, limited local-language support, restricted tool access, and competition with state-backed propaganda; the authors stress that neither regional grouping is monolithic.
qs: Currently, the social and economic benefits of AI are geographically concentrated primarily in the Global North.
For newsrooms in Global South countries however, the challenges are much more pronounced.
Respondents in these countries highlighted knowledge gaps, resource constraints, language barriers, as well as infrastructural, legal, and political challenges.

We opted to use the North-South distinction to extend a power-conscious framing that considers the power dynamics governing AI development and adoption in newsrooms globally, while upholding that the Global North and the Global South are by no means monolithic; as each includes socially and politically diverse countries.

kp.k: Language limitations reproduce unequal access and performance
kp.d: Respondents reported that tools designed principally for English or Western markets performed poorly with non-Western accents, local languages, and cultural contexts. The report connects language coverage to wider inequalities in funding, expertise, connectivity, and locally relevant datasets, while cautioning that even accessible generative tools remain unavailable or impractical in some countries.
qs: Most tools are made for English speakers, which causes accessibility challenges to both non-English speakers and English speakers with non-Western accents.
Voice AI tools do not sound like Africans, [they are] not authentic at all.
Most tools are not applicable to our language or contexts.

GenAI technologies such as ChatGPT are also out of reach for hundreds of millions of people around the world due to accessibility issues such as internet penetration rates, particularly in rural areas.

kp.k: Political conditions shape trust in local AI
kp.d: Some Global South respondents linked distrust of AI to relationships among governments, state-aligned media, and technology institutions. They questioned whether locally developed models use balanced and representative datasets, whether systems will be open or adaptable, and whether independent public-interest outlets can obtain the resources needed to compete.
qs: Scepticism of AI technologies by newsrooms in Global South countries also stems from a distrust in the entities involved in the development and large-scale adoption of AI technologies, such as global technology companies and local, government funded technology and media institutions.
This is a local model, do we trust the datasets used by Arab state institutions?

Arab political realities raise urgent questions about the reliability of [local AI] models. Are they going to be open source? Are they adaptable to Arab newsrooms’ needs? Can newsrooms add their own datasets, for instance?
It is feared that smaller newsrooms that advance public interest and accountability journalism will struggle to survive.

kp.k: AI may widen gaps between organisations
kp.d: Respondents predicted divergent market effects based on organisational size, resources, region, audience, and goals. AI could let small organisations experiment and extend their reach, but could also strengthen already dominant newsrooms, make smaller organisations less sustainable, and create another costly transition for publishers that have not completed digital transformation.
qs: There are concerns that AI will exacerbate sustainability challenges facing less-resourced newsrooms which are still finding their feet, in a highly digitised world and an increasingly AI-powered industry.

AI may empower the smallest of the newsrooms to experiment and reach further than has been possible. AI could also help the large, fortified newsrooms become larger and stronger, snuffing out the little guys.
Different types of news organisations may have different opportunities and threats from AI, depending on their size, resources, audience and goals.
However, small media organisations that will not be able to cope with this transformation will not be able to sustain themselves.

kp.k: Training must span technical and editorial functions
kp.d: Almost 43% of responses emphasised training, while more than 90% highlighted a need for some combination of AI literacy, data literacy, digital storytelling, ethics, prompt engineering, legal awareness, and role-specific instruction. Respondents advocated cross-departmental learning because effective deployment requires journalists, developers, product staff, and data scientists to understand one another’s criteria and constraints.
qs: Almost 43% of responses emphasised the importance of training journalists and other personnel in AI literacy skills and technologies:
The vast majority of responses, more than 90%, highlighted the need for training in a variety of skills and competencies:
We seek to give training in AI-augmented journalism for competences including data literacy, AI literacy, digital storytelling, and ethical considerations.
I would tear down most siloes so that journalists, developers, data scientists and so on work closer together.

kp.k: Collaboration could reduce capability disparities
kp.d: Around 85% welcomed greater collaboration among newsrooms, academia, media organisations, intermediaries, and technology companies. Respondents viewed collaboration as a way to share knowledge and resources, build non-English or locally tailored models, establish responsible-use standards, and reduce gaps between large and small organisations and between Global North and Global South newsrooms, although competition and operational pressures can impede cooperation.
qs: The vast majority welcomed more collaboration between newsrooms and other media organisations and academic institutions, hoping it would help lessen the disparity between small and large newsrooms, as well as regionally between newsrooms in Global North and Global South countries.
More exchange between advanced newsrooms and small newsrooms can be beneficial to bridge knowledge and resources gaps.
We think that collaboration would be specially useful between newsrooms from Global South, such as us.

There is a big gap between the Global North and South. Both of them need to be resilient together and collaborate to expose biases in AI, and have a serious conversation about AI regulations and policies.

kp.k: The report recommends iterative, inclusive AI governance
kp.d: Its six-step roadmap recommends becoming informed, broadening organisation-wide AI literacy, assigning responsibility, testing iteratively with human oversight, creating revisable guidelines, and collaborating externally. The recommendations emphasise cautious experimentation rather than rapid deployment and treat AI governance as an inclusive, continuously reviewed organisational process.
qs: Broaden AI literacy. Everyone needs to understand the components of AI that are impacting journalism the most, because it will impact on everyone’s job – not just editorial, and not just the ‘tech’ people.

Assign responsibility. Someone in your organisation should be given the responsibility of monitoring developments both in your workplace but also more widely, such as assigning AI innovation and R&D leads, and keep a conversation going within your organisation about AI.
Don’t rush to use AI until you are comfortable with the process. Always review the impact.
Draw up guidelines. They can be general or specific. This is a useful learning process when done inclusively to engage all stakeholders. And be prepared to review and change them over time.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI is already used throughout journalism's production chain, although experimentation is much more widespread than substantial organisational impact.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about journalism, not legal services. Beckett and Yaseen report approximately 75% adoption for newsgathering, 90% for news production and 80% for distribution among surveyed organisations. Around 85% had experimented with generative AI. However, only around a quarter reported significant workflow impacts; almost 75% had not yet witnessed a noticeable impact. These are self-reports collected in April–July 2023, not population-wide adoption estimates. Chapter 1's production paragraph calls its 90% figure 'news distribution', but the chart and surrounding discussion assign it to production.

pts.k: Automation can accelerate routine work and free journalists for investigations and other complex editorial tasks.
pts.d: More than half of respondents identified efficiency and productivity as adoption objectives, rather than necessarily demonstrated gains. Chapter 2 also records realised benefits: an anonymous respondent reported saving more than 80% in monitoring and searching for verifiable phrases, without specifying the precise resource measure or evaluation method. Maldita described automation as helping it respond to misinformation at scale after daily WhatsApp queries rose from 200 to over 2,000 during pandemic lockdown. These are organisational experiences, not controlled productivity estimates. Another respondent stressed that speeding production did not necessarily mean improving quality.

pts.k: AI changes distribution work from manual selection and scheduling toward managing rules, recommendations and personalised delivery.
pts.d: Respondents describe recommendation systems, social scheduling, SEO tools, customised content and chatbots as ways to increase reach and engagement. Around a third hoped to improve audience reach or personalisation. An anonymous respondent describes an existing shift from scheduling individual posts to adjusting rules affecting many placements. Maldita's chatbot is a concrete example of automated delivery of previously checked information. These examples establish reported uses and perceived benefits; the report does not provide quantified causal effects on engagement or revenue.

pts.k: Generative AI lowers technical barriers and expands opportunities for drafting, summarisation, coding and content adaptation.
pts.d: Approximately 73% of respondents believed generative AI offered new opportunities. They attributed this partly to accessible interfaces, faster responses and reduced dependence on developers. Reported applications include daily summarisation, headline suggestions, SEO, code snippets and image generation. Some respondents restricted use to analysis or brainstorming rather than publishable content. These are contemporary experiences and expectations in 2023, not benchmarked comparisons with traditional AI. One respondent credits language models with better contextual understanding, while other respondents elsewhere argue that journalistic contextualisation remains a human responsibility; the source contains both positions.

pts.k: Most respondents expect AI use to expand, particularly in disinformation monitoring, personalisation, text generation and preliminary interviewing.
pts.d: Around 80% expected increased newsroom use. Chapter 4 groups anticipated developments into four areas: fact-checking and disinformation analysis; personalisation and automation; summarisation and generation; and chatbots for preliminary interviews and public sentiment. An anonymous respondent forecast adoption of disinformation-monitoring technologies within two to five years of the 2023 survey. Another envisaged chatbots collecting initial accounts, with journalists following up interesting cases. These are plans and predictions, sometimes linked to pilots, rather than completed transformations.

pts.k: AI is changing skill requirements and some roles, but respondents disagree over whether it will reduce employment.
pts.d: Around 60% reported no change yet to existing roles. Others described upskilling journalists in data analysis, algorithm training and prompt design, or creating AI-focused positions. AP reported that automated earnings updates had freed reporters for more meaningful journalism and that it had created three AI-related roles. Forecasts diverge: some respondents anticipate leaner newsrooms and fewer writers; others expect augmentation and increased demand for people who use AI effectively. The authors conclude that some jobs will be replaced and others created, but offer no aggregate employment forecast or deadline.

pts.k: Efficiency gains depend on integration, resources, training and audience value; AI adoption can initially add work or fail to deliver useful products.
pts.d: Respondents cite limited funding, scarce expertise, compatibility problems, weak onboarding and managerial structures as obstacles. Experienced organisations increasingly focus on interoperability, while less-resourced organisations struggle to acquire basic capabilities. One respondent predicts additional adaptation work during adoption. A concrete negative case is an automated stock-performance story service discontinued because users preferred stock graphs and pandemic volatility triggered excessive alerts. These accounts qualify claims of automatic efficiency or commercial benefit.

pts.k: Human verification and editorial judgement remain necessary because AI can fabricate information, reproduce bias and mishandle context.
pts.d: The authors explain that generative models sometimes make up facts. Respondents describe human review as a condition of reliance and generally support augmentation rather than autonomous editorial decision-making. One reports tests yielding nonexistent content; another says claim-matching systems struggle when a statement's truth changes over time. Some organisations avoid direct editorial applications altogether. The evidence is qualitative experience and professional judgement, not measured hallucination rates or proof that any particular review process eliminates errors.

pts.k: Generative AI may increase misinformation's scale and make fabricated media harder to check.
pts.d: Respondents fear larger-scale production and distribution of disinformation and argue that fully synthetic content is harder to debunk than manipulated originals because there may be no reference material. Some expect this to damage news consumption, while one also predicts a possible turn toward trusted sources. These are risk forecasts without quantified incidence or timelines. Respondents were divided about whether generative AI creates distinct challenges: 40% said yes, 52% were unsure and 8% said no; some instead saw familiar risks becoming more severe.

pts.k: Commercial incentives could make AI adoption produce more low-quality content and weaken trust, while responsible journalism may gain comparative value.
pts.d: Interviewed respondents fear that competition for clicks and revenue will encourage mass-produced content, biased commentary and weaker editorial standards. These are conditional predictions and concerns, not measured audience responses. In their conclusion, Beckett and Yaseen argue that human policy and ethical choices shape outcomes: AI can facilitate clickbait or support more human-centred journalism. They also identify potential disintermediation if audiences obtain information from chatbots instead of news outlets.

pts.k: AI may empower small newsrooms but also widen competitive and regional inequalities.
pts.d: The authors characterise AI's benefits as concentrated in the Global North, drawing on regional survey accounts and cited literature about the AI divide and global inclusion. Respondents describe constraints involving capital, connectivity, scarce technical staff, language support, accents and local cultural context. Some predict that organisations unable to adapt will become unsustainable; others see affordable generative AI as potentially expanding small-newsroom capabilities. The report treats these as competing possibilities, with outcomes dependent on resources, location and access. Collaboration and local-language model development are proposed mitigations, not demonstrated solutions.

pts.k: Reliance on technology providers can increase dependency, concentrate gatekeeping power and import providers' values into journalism.
pts.d: Respondents acknowledge that technology companies supply useful, sometimes accessible tools, but predict that dependence on proprietary systems can subject newsrooms to commercial priorities, opaque training data and externally imposed values. MENA respondents additionally describe distrust of government-linked models and concern that well-funded, government-aligned media will gain advantages over independent public-interest outlets. These claims combine institutional experience and prospective concerns; the report does not quantify resulting market concentration or media capture.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central evidence is a non-representative international survey supplemented by interviews and conversations, with illustrative cases rather than controlled tests.
pts.d: The report covers 105 news and media organisations in 46 countries, with respondents including journalists, technologists and managers. Only 16 organisations also participated in the 2019 survey, so comparisons should not be read as a stable longitudinal panel. Most quotations are anonymised and some lightly edited. Survey percentages record adoption reports, experiences or expectations, depending on the question. The regional analysis additionally cites published research. The project was funded by the Google News Initiative; the report states that editorial responsibility remained with its author.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source is a 2023 snapshot of rapid experimentation, with mostly undated predictions and explicit uncertainty about longer-term outcomes.
pts.d: The surveys and interviews took place in April–July 2023. Generative-AI experience was therefore relatively recent, and the authors say most newsrooms had not had enough time for comprehensive assessments. Historical examples include pandemic-era misinformation workflows and AP's earlier earnings-report automation. The clearest numerical forecast horizon is one respondent's two-to-five-year expectation for disinformation-monitoring adoption. Other forecasts use 'the future', 'the next few years' or the adoption phase. Realising benefits is repeatedly conditioned on editorial oversight, integration, resources, skills and organisational choices.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The effects span journalists, technical and audience teams, competing media organisations and the public, with uneven exposure by resources and language.
pts.d: Reporters and editors face automation of routine tasks, new checking responsibilities, upskilling and possible job substitution. Engineers, data scientists and AI managers may see new demand and more cross-departmental work. Distribution and product teams increasingly manage automated delivery and personalisation. Small, local, independent and Global South newsrooms face distinctive financial, infrastructural and language constraints; larger organisations may consolidate advantages. Audiences may receive faster, tailored information but also face synthetic misinformation, biased representation and uncertain trust signals. Marginalised communities and speakers of under-supported languages are singled out as particularly vulnerable. No direct claim about lawyers, law firms or legal markets is made.
